DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekly Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study (Thornbury District Council)

The author's case for approval rests on five claims:
- **Local evidence.** A six-month pilot with 4,000 households across mixed wards.
- **Uniform service.** Participation held up across houses and flats, so one service fits all.
- **Complete costing.** Every cost line is shown, and the disposal saving uses actual and quoted rates.
- **Fully funded.** The net cost of about £490,000 is covered by the £520,000 provisional allocation.
- **Local treatment** at Brookfield, with a timetable worked back from the vehicle lead time.

The pilot is a genuine strength, and the cost arithmetic in Table 2 is correct. But the uniform-service claim, the tonnage projection, the treatment arrangement and the "fully funded" conclusion are all contradicted by figures in the paper itself.

## 1. Participation differs sharply between houses and flats

Table 1 gives participation of **66% in houses and 21% in flats**. Flats participate at about a third of the rate of houses.

The paper says participation was "broadly similar across housing types", and the author says it "held up across houses and flats". The table contradicts both, and it is the paper's own data, so this point is settled.

It matters for more than wording. The recommendation of a single uniform service rests on this claim. A 21% rate in flats suggests they need a different approach: communal containers, bin-store placement, or targeted engagement. The statutory duty covers flats as well, so the low rate can't simply be accepted.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate that isn't in the pilot data

Section 3 applies "the pilot's **64%** participation rate". The pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and 64% appears nowhere in Table 1.

The pilot's mix of flats (800 of 4,000, or 20%) matches the district's (about 20%). That is a real strength of the pilot design, and it means the pilot rates can be applied directly by housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ≈ 2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ≈ 160 |
| **District** | **52,000** | | | **≈ 2,870** |

The paper's 3,290 tonnes is overstated by about **13%**. The tonnage feeds directly into the disposal saving.

## 3. Brookfield can't take all the food waste

Section 4 says Brookfield can take **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. That is below both the paper's projection of 3,290 tonnes and the corrected figure of about 2,870. Roughly **1,070 tonnes a year** (about 37% of the corrected projection) has no treatment route at the £38 gate fee. The only alternative named is a plant **46 miles away**, with no gate fee quoted and no haulage costed.

The author's statement that "treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away" is therefore true for only about 63% of the tonnage. The rest also affects whether six vehicles are enough, since longer trips to tip waste take crew time.

## 4. With these corrections, "fully funded" doesn't hold

Table 2's arithmetic is correct: vehicles £990,000 ÷ 7 ≈ £141,400, crews 12 × £34,000 = £408,000, total £733,400. The disposal saving of £74 per tonne is also right. What changes the net cost is how many tonnes the saving applies to:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | vs £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paper (3,290 t, all at Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,000 | £30k headroom |
| Corrected tonnage, ignoring the cap | ≈ £212,000 | ≈ £521,000 | Roughly break-even |
| Corrected tonnage, Brookfield cap (1,800 t) | ≈ £133,000 | ≈ £600,000 **plus** treatment of ~1,070 t at an unknown cost | **At least ~£80k short** |

The third row reflects the arrangements the paper actually describes. Two further points:
- The allocation is **provisional**, so even the paper's own figures rest on funding that isn't confirmed.
- Several costs are missing from Table 2 (§5 below), and all of them would widen the gap.

## 5. Costs not in Table 2

The author says "every cost line is shown". Missing or unclear items include:
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** described in §6.
- **Haulage and gate fees** for tonnage that can't go to Brookfield.
- **A spare vehicle and cover crews.** Six vehicles for six rounds leaves no margin for breakdowns, leave or sickness.
- **Supervision, management, insurance, recruitment and training.**
- **Whether £34,000 per operative includes on-costs** such as employer NI and pension. If it is salary only, crew costs are understated by roughly a quarter.
- **Vehicle financing costs.** Depreciation alone omits interest. And £990,000 for vehicles plus the caddies for 52,000 households is an **upfront capital outlay**. Annualising the costs doesn't show Cabinet that cash need.

## 6. Timetable and compliance

- **No margin in the timetable.** Vehicles arrive in March, crews train on them in March, and collections start on 5 April. Any delay in vehicle delivery postpones the launch, and there is no contingency plan. The vehicle order also needs Cabinet approval before the December deadline.
- **Statutory deadline.** My understanding is that England's Simpler Recycling rules required weekly food waste collections from **31 March 2026** for most councils, with transitional arrangements for some. A launch in April 2027 would be a year after that. Please check whether Thornbury is covered by a transitional arrangement, and say so in the paper. I'm fairly but not fully confident of the date, so verify it against the regulations.

## What holds up

- **The pilot design.** It is a real local trial, weekly measurement by housing type, and a housing mix that matches the district. That is better evidence than most feasibility studies have, and it is what makes the corrections above possible.
- **Low contamination**, under 2% by weight from spot checks at the plant.
- **The arithmetic in Tables 1 and 2**, and the diversion saving of £74 per tonne.
- **Resident satisfaction** of 81% is encouraging. The paper should report the survey response rate, though, since participating households are probably more likely to respond.

## What is open, and what would settle it

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Where do the ~1,070 t above Brookfield's cap go, and at what cost? | A quote from the 46-mile plant or another, with haulage and vehicle-time costs |
| What's the real net cost? | A revised Table 2: corrected tonnage, all treatment routes, the missing cost lines, capital shown separately |
| Is the £520k allocation confirmed? | Confirmation from government, or a plan for any shortfall |
| How to serve flats | An options appraisal (communal bins, bin-store caddies, targeted engagement), ideally piloted |
| Statutory position | Legal confirmation of the deadline and of any transitional arrangement |
| Vehicle numbers | Round modelling that includes the longer haul and a spare vehicle |

## Recommendation

This is not a choice between rolling out the service and not rolling it out. The duty is statutory, so the service has to happen. Cabinet should be asked to approve a corrected plan, not this one.

1. **Correct the paper:** the participation claim, the 57% rate, a tonnage of about 2,870, the Brookfield cap, and the full costs.
2. **Present the funding position honestly:** a likely gap, and how it will be met.
3. **Consider approving the vehicle order separately** before December to protect the timetable, provided round modelling confirms the number of vehicles, including a spare.
4. **Add a flats-specific approach** to the roll-out.
